name: Bản Giốc Waterfall
summary: One of the largest waterfalls in Asia. The Quây Sơn River spills over limestone in wide tiers here, on the border between Vietnam and China.

hero.alt: The tiers of the Bản Giốc waterfall

eras.label: Long ago
eras.title: Water over limestone
eras.text: The Quây Sơn River has spent thousands of years dissolving and depositing limestone, forming the wide steps of rock that the water now pours over. The falls are about 30 m high and more than 200 m wide.

image.alt: Water pouring over the limestone steps

eras.title: A border settled
eras.text: The waterfall sits right on the border: the Chinese side calls it Detian. In 2009 the two countries finished marking their land border, and the falls are shared between them.

image.alt: The falls seen from the Chinese side

eras.title: Part of a Global Geopark
eras.text: UNESCO recognised the Non Nước Cao Bằng Geopark, which includes the waterfall, caves and karst valleys of the province.

eras.title: A shared scenic area
eras.text: Vietnam and China opened a cooperative scenic area at the falls, where visitors could cross a short way into the other side on a trial basis.

eras.label: Today
eras.title: Rafts below the spray
eras.text: Bamboo rafts carry visitors close to the foot of the falls, into the cool spray. The water is fullest from June to September.

image.alt: The tiers of the Bản Giốc waterfall

story.title: Pác Bó, 1941

image.alt: The green valleys of Cao Bằng

story.narration: In January 1941, a man in his fifties crossed the mountains from China into Cao Bằng. It was Nguyễn Ái Quốc, soon to be known as Ho Chi Minh, coming home after thirty years abroad. He lived in a small cave at Pác Bó, near the border, sleeping on a bed of planks and working at a stone table by the stream. He named the stream after Lenin and a nearby mountain after Karl Marx. From here he organised the Việt Minh, the movement that would declare independence four years later.

story.title: The tiger cave
story.narration: A few kilometres from the waterfall lies a large cave called Ngườm Ngao. In the Tày language the name means 'tiger cave'. The story goes that tigers once lived there and villagers did not dare to enter. Today a path leads through chambers of stalactites and stalagmites that local people have named after the shapes they see in them: a field of rice terraces, a golden curtain, a pair of hands at prayer.

story.title: Chestnuts and bánh cuốn
story.narration: Ask anyone in the north what to bring back from Cao Bằng and they will say chestnuts from Trùng Khánh. They are small and sweet, roasted in the autumn by roadside sellers. Cao Bằng also has its own way of eating bánh cuốn, the thin steamed rice rolls. Here they come with a bowl of hot bone broth instead of a cold dipping sauce, a breakfast made for cold mountain mornings.

guide.price: Entry ticket to the scenic area. Bamboo raft rides to the foot of the falls cost extra.

hours.notes: Approximate. The falls are best seen in the morning light.

do: Wear a life jacket on the bamboo rafts.
Bring a rain jacket for the spray near the falls.
Visit Ngườm Ngao cave on the same trip.
Carry your passport if you plan to enter the shared border area.
dont: Cross the border markers outside the official scenic area.
Climb on wet rocks near the falls.
Fly a drone. It is a border zone.

tips.title: Cao Bằng food
tips.text: Try roast duck with mắc mật leaves, bánh cuốn with bone broth, and roasted Trùng Khánh chestnuts in autumn.

tips.title: Getting there
tips.text: Cao Bằng city is about 6–7 hours by bus from Hà Nội; the falls are another 2 hours east.

tips.title: Combine with
tips.text: Pác Bó historic site, on the way back to the city, and the Phật Tích Trúc Lâm pagoda above the falls.
